29.0.0.en: 1 In the tenth year, in the tenth month, in the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, set thy face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him, and against all Egypt: 3 Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great crocodile that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself. 4 But I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales. 5 And I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness, thee and all the fish of thy rivers: thou shalt fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered: I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of the heaven. 6 And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD, because they have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel. 7 When they took hold of thee by thy hand, thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder: and when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins to be at a stand."

29.0.1.en: The prophet Ezekiel dates this prophecy to the tenth year of the captivity, when Pharaoh advanced with his armies toward Jerusalem to deliver it from the siege. The men of Judah did not listen to the warnings of Jeremiah or Ezekiel, but leaned upon Pharaoh against Babylon, and rose in revolt against Babylon, and the Pharaoh of Egypt went out to rescue them from Babylon... which led afterward to the destruction of the city and the killing of many.

29.1.0.en: God offered the fitting comparison. Since Tyre was an island rich in its trade and proud of its merchants, He likened it to a ship, precious in the materials of its building and its cargo, and perfect in its crew and its guards. But Pharaoh of Egypt relied, with his men, on the Nile of Egypt, which made Egypt fertile; therefore He likened him to the great crocodile that lies in the midst of his rivers [3], for the river Nile was famous for its crocodiles.

29.1.1.en: God called Pharaoh "the great crocodile" perhaps because the Egyptians worshiped crocodiles and so became crocodiles, and their king was called "the great crocodile." He who worships stones becomes a stone, and he who worships vanity becomes vanity, and he who worships the true God becomes "true" and enjoys partnership in the divine nature.

29.1.2.en: The sin of Tyre was its exploitation of the fall of Judah and its greedy seizing of this opportunity, but the sin of Pharaoh was pride, for with his strong army he thought he was able to do everything, "which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself" [3]. It is said that by this was meant Pharaoh Khafra, who boasted of two things: that he himself made with his own hands the power and security he enjoyed, and that this was for his own sake. He set up the "ego" as a god, as the maker of the river, the secret of Egypt's fertility and greatness, and said it made this for its own sake. The historian Herodotus relates of this king that he reigned in great prosperity for twenty-five years, and his heart was lifted up by his success, saying that God Himself could not remove him from his kingdom. The prophet Jeremiah spoke of this pride thus: "Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers? Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof" (Jer 46:7-8).

29.1.3.en: What does God do with this proud crocodile who thinks he is the creator of the river for his own account?!

29.1.4.en: He says: "I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales.

29.1.5.en: And I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness, thee and all the fish of thy rivers.

29.1.6.en: Thou shalt fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered.

29.2.0.en: I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of the heaven" [4-5].

29.2.1.en: Since in the pride of his heart he thought that the power and prosperity he had were the work of his own hands, God deprives him of these blessings and drives him out from the midst of his rivers, to die as a fish dies outside the water. And since he thought that everything was created to serve himself, with everything working for his service and his account, he is cast into the wilderness; he dies with none to ask after him and none to bury him, becoming prey for the beasts of the field and food for the fowls of the heaven! And since he gathered around him many who took refuge in him or fought with him, they become like the fish sticking to his scales; whether nations or commanders, chariots or army, they receive the same fate. Thus pride robs him of his goods and his honor and even his life, and humbles even those who cling to him and rely on him. It is said that this Pharaoh went out to fight the people of Cyrene, who had driven out his friend Aricius, king of Libya, in order to restore him to his kingdom; but the Egyptians rebelled against him in his absence, so neither he nor his commanders returned to his kingdom, and he was cast into the wilderness with them.

29.2.2.en: This is the work of pride in the life of one who belongs to the greatest heavenly order (the devil), who by his pride lost heaven and fell to the abyss; in place of divine friendship he entered into enmity with God, and in place of heavenly glory he entered into perpetual humiliation. He was shattered and shattered with him many of his angels and also of human beings! By the same disease our first parents fell from paradise and were deprived of continual existence in the divine presence, and bequeathed to their offspring all toil and misery! We were driven out from the river of life, and cast into the wilderness of this life, to die spiritually and become the prey of all the beasts of the field (the demon of injustice and cruelty) and the fowls of the heaven (the demon of pride).

29.3.0.en: He returns to liken Pharaoh of Egypt to a staff of reed to the house of Israel [6]; he is like a staff, but of reed (cane), which breaks when a man leans upon it, and the shoulder of the one who leans on it is torn and weakened. Instead of supporting him, it shatters his strength, as the prophet Isaiah says: "For Egypt helps in vain and to no purpose; therefore have I called her Rahab that sitteth still" (Isa 30:7). Pharaoh of Egypt encouraged King Zedekiah to revolt against Babylon, to betray the covenant and break the oath, so Hezekiah was lost, Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah were shattered, and Pharaoh was defeated.

29.3.1.en: It should be noted here that the discipline of Pharaoh and the fish sticking to his scales was by leaving them to die in the wilderness, to be eaten by the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven. This is the most hideous death, which the Egyptians hated, for they were anxious for the body and built tombs to preserve it until the spirit should return to clothe itself again with its body.

29.4.0.en: 8 "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring a sword upon thee, and cut off man and beast out of thee. 9 And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste; and they shall know that I am the LORD: because he hath said, The river is mine, and I have made it. 10 Behold, therefore I am against thee, and against thy rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt utterly waste and desolate, from Migdol to Syene, even unto the border of Cush. 11 No foot of man shall pass through it, nor foot of beast shall pass through it, neither shall it be inhabited forty years. 12 And I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate, and her cities among the cities that are laid waste shall be desolate forty years: and I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries."

29.4.1.en: In the pride of his heart Pharaoh thought that he was the maker of the great river and the defender of the nations around him, but the Lord brings a sword upon him and cuts off man and beast. Through pride man loses his humanity, "his intellectual life," and also his animal nature, "his earthly life"; he loses what belongs to mind and body together. The extent of this loss is a complete loss, stretching from the north, "Migdol," to the south, "Syene," on the border of Cush.

29.4.2.en: "Migdol" is a Semitic name meaning "tower"; it was most probably a fortified city on the northeastern border of Egypt toward Palestine, now Tell el-Her, twelve miles west of Pelusium. It lies on the road by which the Jews passed during their exodus from Egypt.

29.4.3.en: Syene, in Egyptian Sewen, is on the eastern bank of the river on the southern border of Egypt. Opposite it on the other side is "Elephantine Island." It was a source of granite for the Egyptian statues, and also a strong center of defense on the southern border.

29.4.4.en: As for Cush, it most often means "Ethiopia" or "Abyssinia," and here it means the land of Nubia.

29.4.5.en: So the discipline of Pharaoh of Egypt is a comprehensive discipline, in which his land becomes a ruin where neither man nor beast dwells, extending from the far south; but at the same time it is temporary and for a fixed period (forty years), unlike the other nations, for whom the decree was that the discipline be everlasting. He scatters and disperses the Egyptians for a time. Perhaps this is a reference to the confidence which Egypt holds in the heart of God after accepting faith in the Lord Christ, for He says through the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt... And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it" (Isa 19).

29.4.6.en: She spends the days of her idolatry like one wandering in the wilderness, so that she may return to faith in God her Savior and worship Him.

29.5.s.en: 3. The return and restoration of Egypt:

29.5.0.en: 13 "Yet thus saith the Lord GOD; At the end of forty years will I gather the Egyptians from the people whither they were scattered: 14 And I will bring again the captivity of Egypt, and will cause them to return into the land of Pathros, into the land of their birth; and they shall be there a base kingdom. 15 It shall be the basest of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations: for I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations. 16 And it shall be no more the confidence of the house of Israel, which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance, when they shall look after them: but they shall know that I am the Lord GOD."

29.6.0.en: The Lord gave Pharaoh of Egypt a lesson, he who stirred up the king of Judah and made him not listen to the voice of the prophets; instead of supporting him, he and his people were scattered for forty years, and then He restored the kingdom of Egypt to Pathros, the land of Pathros [14], an Egyptian word meaning "the land of the south." By Pathros is meant Upper Egypt, as opposed to "Lower and Middle Egypt"; Lower Egypt, or the Delta, was more desirable than Upper Egypt. It should be noted that after Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem captive, some Jews settled in Pathros (Jer 44:1-2, 15).

29.6.1.en: It is as though by the return of the kingdom to "Pathros" He means its weakness and its inability to make war and to support others, so that it does not return again to its pride, and does not deceive the people of God by being a support for them against Babylon.

29.7.s.en: 4. His being delivered to the king of Babylon:

29.7.0.en: 17 And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth year, in the first month, in the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 18 "Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled: yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it: 19 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey; and it shall be the wages for his army. 20 I have given him the land of Egypt for his labour wherewith he served against it, because they wrought for me, saith the Lord GOD. 21 In that day will I cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth, and I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them; and they shall know that I am the LORD."

29.7.1.en: Finally, instead of defending Judah, Pharaoh of Egypt falls into the grasp of the king of Babylon, who takes his wealth and seizes him as spoil and plunders him. The Lord delivers him to the king of Babylon as a recompense for what he did to Tyre. Tyre had seized Jerusalem and plundered it, so God stirred up Babylon against it, and when it had destroyed Tyre He rewarded it with the wealth of Pharaoh. Nebuchadnezzar attacked Egypt in the thirty-seventh year of his reign (568-567 B.C.) and took much from it, but it did not become part of his kingdom.

29.8.0.en: But the main subject is not the reward of the king of Babylon, who destroyed Tyre that had gloated over Jerusalem; rather, what occupies the mind of God is to raise up a horn (that is, a power) for the salvation of His people [21] and to open the mouth of His prophet in the midst of the people to proclaim this salvation in a spirit of hope and joy, for He says: "I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them; and they shall know that I am the LORD" [21].

29.8.1.en: My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself!

29.8.2.en: * Pharaoh of Egypt prides himself on the river Nile, and counts it his river, which his hands made for himself!

29.8.3.en: How strange is man, who ascribes to himself what belongs to his God, and instead of giving thanks and praise to God, the Creator of the world for his sake, thinks himself a god!

29.8.4.en: * You disciplined Egypt for a time, and You came to her, O Savior, as upon a light cloud!

29.8.5.en: You shattered her idols and set up Your altar in her midst!

29.8.6.en: * Hasten, O Savior, to my soul!

29.8.7.en: Let the idols of my heart tremble before Your presence!

29.8.8.en: And let Your divine altar be set up within me!

29.8.9.en: * Take away from me ingratitude and teach me thanksgiving!

29.8.10.en: The river Nile is the work of Your hands!

29.8.11.en: Your gifts are more than can be counted!

29.8.12.en: What shall I render unto You, O Lord, for the multitude of Your kindnesses?!

30.0.0.en: 1 The word of the LORD came again unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Howl ye, Woe worth the day! 3 For the day is near, even the day of the LORD is near, a cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen. 4 And the sword shall come upon Egypt, and great pain shall be in Cush, when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down. 5 Cush, and Put, and Lud, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. 6 Thus saith the LORD; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down: from Migdol to Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord GOD. 7 And she shall be desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate, and her cities shall be in the midst of the cities that are wasted. 8 And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be destroyed. 9 In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh."

30.1.0.en: When the Lord asked the prophet Ezekiel to prophesy against Pharaoh of Egypt, He did not direct the call to howl to Pharaoh nor to all the people of Egypt, but directed it as a general call to the whole pagan world, since Pharaoh of Egypt represented it at that time, saying, "Howl ye, Woe worth the day!" [2]. And He called the day of Pharaoh "the day of the LORD," because it is a discipline from the Lord upon all the nations! Therefore it was said: "I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit" (Ezek 31:16); "And they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall" (Ezek 32:10). Thus the news of his fall resounds in the whole world, and all creation trembles at it.

30.1.1.en: It must be noted that Pharaoh here points to "Satan," as the instigator of rebellion against the prophetic words, who thinks himself a possessor of authority, able to support many. We spoke of Pharaoh as a symbol of Satan in our study of the Book of Exodus, in his resistance to the prophet Moses and Aaron. As Origen says: [In my opinion, some names of peoples or kings that we read of in the Holy Bible undoubtedly belong to the evil angels or the opposing powers, such as Pharaoh king of Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and Assyria].

30.1.2.en: If Pharaoh, as a symbol of Satan, thinks himself a possessor of authority to whom the other nations resort and in whom they take refuge, God proclaims his psychological defeat and his shattering by fear. He made his day "a cloudy day" [2]. The cloud, as we saw before, is a sign of the divine glory; it covers the holy mountain or the holy tent or the temple, declaring man's entrance into invisible mysteries that cannot be grasped. But for Satan or Pharaoh the cloud represents a state of darkness, in which he cannot act and does not know what to do. If he thought himself a leader, he walks in the darkness and stumbles, and those who cling to him and shelter under his wings stumble with him. Therefore He says: "In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh" [9]. The nearest nation to him is "Cush," by which perhaps Nubia is meant, and also some regions in Asia. In any case, terror filled the heart of Pharaoh, and even the heart of the nearest kingdom to him that sheltered under his shadow; so what will be the fate of the other, distant nations?! The one who terrified them is the Lord Himself: "messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid," because she left the Lord and resorted to Pharaoh.

30.2.0.en: With the fall of Pharaoh and his terror, "Cush (Nubia or Ethiopia), and Put, and Lud, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them" [5].

30.2.1.en: We have already spoken of Cush and also of Put and Lud (Ezek 27:10); as for his saying "all the mingled people," some translate it "the mixed people" and others "Arabia"...

30.2.2.en: As for Chub, some see it as Lub (Libya), most probably a people who dwelt in northeastern Africa, and the Septuagint has: "the Libyans." "The men of the land that is in league" means the countries that entered into a covenant with Pharaoh for their protection, especially against the attack of the king of Babylon.

30.3.0.en: The pride of the devil must be brought down completely throughout his whole kingdom, from the far north (Migdol) to the far south (Syene) [6], and he collapses with all his helpers and those joined to him: "And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be destroyed" [8].

30.4.0.en: 10 "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also make the wealth of Egypt to cease by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon. 11 He and his people with him, the terrible of the nations, shall be brought to destroy the land: and they shall draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain. 12 And I will make the rivers dry, and sell the land into the hand of the wicked: and I will make the land waste, and all that is therein, by the hand of strangers: I the LORD have spoken it. 13 Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt. 14 And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No. 15 And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No. 16 And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily. 17 The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity. 18 At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity. 19 Thus will I execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I am the LORD."

30.5.0.en: In place of pride and arrogance, fear and trembling come upon Pharaoh and all the surrounding nations that sheltered in him. And in place of his riches and wealth, as he said, "My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself" (Ezek 29:3, 9), the rivers become dry [12]. And in place of his kingship and authority, He delivers his land into the hand of the wicked strangers [12]. In place of security and rest, the Lord sets a fire, and his kingdom loses its hope, for it loses its youth in the war, and its daughters in captivity! He thought himself a god, and behold, his idols and his worship are shattered [13].

30.5.1.en: The kingdom of the devil must come to an end; his awe and his deceptive fear vanish, all his capacities collapse, and he is cast into the eternal fire with all who followed him and took refuge in him.

30.5.2.en: All the centers of power that worked for his service under his authority will be shattered, which are symbolized by the fortified Egyptian cities mentioned here, the most important of which are:

30.6.0.en: a. Noph: "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt" [13]. When He wished to speak of the destruction of all the authority of Pharaoh (a symbol of Satan) and the end of his kingdom, so that no prince of his appears any more, He chose "Noph" (in Hebrew), which in Egyptian is "Menefer" or "Minfri," and in Greek "Memphis" Μέμφις, and is counted the most famous city in Egypt. Menes built it when he united Lower and Upper Egypt, and it became the capital of ancient Egypt; only Thebes rivaled it in size and importance, until the Greeks built the city of Alexandria as a capital.

30.6.1.en: Memphis is about ten miles south of Cairo, beside Mit Rahina. The palaces of the kings were built inside the capital Memphis or beside it, and the pyramids were built near it, twelve miles south of the center of the ruins of Memphis, and in them the kings were buried.

30.6.2.en: After the building of Alexandria, Memphis took second place, and it was crowded with inhabitants until the Arabs entered Egypt, when it quickly fell into ruin. The growth of Fustat and Cairo went hand in hand with the ruin of Memphis, since the stones and building materials were carried off from Memphis.

30.6.3.en: The bull Apis was worshiped in Memphis as sacred to the god Ptah, the chief god of the city, "the god of fire."

30.7.0.en: b. Pathros [14]: We said that it is "the land of the south," meaning Upper Egypt; as He destroys the idols from Memphis in Lower Egypt, so He lays waste Upper Egypt.

30.7.1.en: c. Zoan [14]: On the eastern bank of the Delta, built seven years after Hebron (Num 13:22). The fields of Zoan are mentioned in (Ps 78:12, 43) as the place where the wonders connected with the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt were wrought, and it is mentioned in (Isa 19:11, 13; 30:4) perhaps as the capital of Egypt. It was known by the name "Avaris" as the capital of the Hyksos; it was neglected after their expulsion, but attention was restored to it in the Ramesside period, in the days of the reign of Seti I and Ramesses II, and it bore the name "Raamses" (Ex 1:11); its Greek name is "Tanis," and it is now called "San el-Hagar."

30.8.0.en: d. No: He says that God executes His judgments on No and cuts off its multitude [15].

30.8.1.en: No, No-Amon, Amon-No: an Egyptian name meaning the city of Amon. He was the greatest of the gods of Egypt, especially from the seventeenth dynasty. (The word Amon in Egyptian means the hidden or concealed one, and in Hebrew it means amen or the maker.)

30.8.2.en: No-Amon, which is the city of Thebes, lies in Upper Egypt, 400 miles south of Memphis, on both banks of the Nile. Ahmose gave it great importance by expelling the Hyksos, liberating Egypt, reunifying it, and laying the foundation stone of the Egyptian empire that the 18th and 19th dynasties built. His successors cared for the city, and it grew in splendor and magnificence. It had a hundred gates, and its priest, the priest of Amon, was counted the second man in the state. Even when Memphis later became the capital of Egypt, Thebes kept its importance because of the worship of the god Amon and the wealth it contained in temples, buildings, and obelisks. In the seventh century B.C., Esarhaddon the Syrian conqueror reached it in 671 B.C., and his son Ashurbanipal conquered and occupied it in 664 B.C. (Nah 3:8), but did not destroy it completely. When it led the revolt of Upper Egypt against the Romans, the Roman armies destroyed it and it became a collection of ruins. That region still bears witness, at Luxor, Karnak, Qurna, Medinet Habu, the tombs of the kings, Deir el-Bahari, and so on, to the greatness of those monuments, which draw the eyes of the whole world as a museum of the greatest human civilization that history has seen.

30.8.3.en: e. Sin: "And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt" [15]; "Sin shall have great pain" [16]. It is the only city placed at the disposal of the Assyrian; it was undoubtedly in the place of Pelusium, to keep the gates of Egypt open before the Assyrian king.

30.8.4.en: It was called the strength of Egypt because many battles were fought at it. Its site is now Tell el-Farama, 20 miles northeast of Qantara.

30.9.0.en: f. Aven: "The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity" [17].

30.9.1.en: The city of On (Aven), in Egyptian "Iunu" and in Greek "Heliopolis." The seat of the sun god Ra. It is now Tell Hassan, or Ain Shams, seven miles northeast of Cairo; there was found the house of the father-in-law of Joseph (Gen 41:45, 50).

30.9.2.en: Its temple was of great importance, the kings loved it, and its priests were the most learned of priests; therefore a tradition exists that Plato and many of the Greek philosophers studied at Heliopolis.

30.9.3.en: It is as though God wished to declare that the young men of this city of learning fall by the sword and its existence comes to an end, for learning without faith does not build up the soul.

30.9.5.en: An Egyptian name meaning "the house of the goddess Bast" (Pi-Bastis); its Greek name is "Bubastis." It is now called Tell Basta, beside Zagazig, east of the Delta.

30.10.0.en: h. Tehaphnehes: "And the fire shall grow dark in Tehaphnehes, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her" [18]. It is the city to which some Jews resorted when they fled to Egypt after the killing of Gedaliah (Jer 43:7). In Greek it is called "Daphne," now "Tell Defenneh," 10 miles west of Qantara; in the Septuagint it is "Taphnis," and its meaning is "the fortress or citadel of Penahse." Penahse was most probably a commander with authority from Thebes, who lived in the 11th century B.C. and led a revolt in the north, so several cities arose bearing his name.

30.10.1.en: Herodotus mentions that Daphnae was the fortress of Egypt on the Asian side, and that the Greeks guarded it. In its ruins were found many Greek pottery vessels and also iron weapons and arrowheads of bronze and iron bearing a Greek character, besides many remains that bear witness that it was a huge trade route.

30.11.0.en: 20 And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 21 "Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword. 22 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken; and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand. 23 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries. 24 And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword in his hand: but I will break Pharaoh's arms, and he shall groan before him with the groanings of a deadly wounded man. 25 But I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh shall fall down; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt. 26 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them among the countries; and they shall know that I am the LORD."

30.11.1.en: Having spoken of the ruin that befell his fortified cities, he begins to speak of his arm, how a deadly wound struck it that cannot be healed, so that he can no longer bear a weapon, neither to defend himself nor those who sheltered in him. At the same time God strengthens the arms of the king of Babylon and puts the sword in his hand to discipline Pharaoh of Egypt, so that his hands fall and his people are scattered!

30.11.2.en: This is a picture of the satanic work that resists the divine plan, which ends in complete failure, however successful it may appear at the beginning.

30.11.3.en: Fire in the city of fire!

30.11.4.en: * The Egyptians worshiped the god Ptah in Memphis, the city of the god of fire!

30.11.5.en: And Pharaoh thought that he was the fiery man, the possessor of authority, to whom the nations resort and he protects them.

30.11.6.en: Behold, the Lord makes the day of Pharaoh a day of cloud, a day of darkness and fear, so his spirit is shattered, and terror falls on all Egypt!

30.11.7.en: God kindles the fire of His discipline and breaks all the powers of Pharaoh!

30.11.8.en: * Instead of protecting others, he becomes a terror!

30.11.9.en: He loses his wealth and his arms are shattered!

30.11.10.en: * Teach me, O Lord, the spirit of humility!

30.11.11.en: You are a refuge for me and for my brethren!

30.11.12.en: I and they need Your protection and Your care, O wise Shepherd of souls!
